item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
Good assessment of the on the ground reality for security in most large enterprises right now. The fragmented landscape of the risk surface is only going to get more gnarly, making it even more complex for enterprises to solve.
There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure, data, and code to secure. Most large enterprises can barely keep up with this, let alone smaller startups or most companies outside of tech.
In many cases enterprises need to work to modernize their tech stacks. Data, in most organizations, is highly fragmented which means you don’t really know the state of risk at any given time. Some systems are open up privileges too broadly, and others are operating primarily via security through obscurity. Lots of upgrading here to do.
Once you can get your data and infra into a better spot, at least you have a chance for agents to help you secure the environment. Agent swarms can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months, and none of it would be possible before we had long running agents and computer use good enough.
This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability.
But everyone does need to do the hard work of getting the basics right at the start.

item.title: The Changing Physics of Cybersecurity and Drug Development with OpenAI President Greg Brockman
item.description:
播客：No Priors
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:19 To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we think that humans should be firmly in the driver's seat, should have control over the future, and this technology should amplify human agency. When I look at the world we're going to be in, where software in some ways is becoming like the barrier to entry, it's becoming so cheap. You don't just want software. Right? You want software that is reliable, that is secure, that you can believe in.
Speaker 1 | 00:19 - 00:32 And so cyber spend, security spend should actually vastly outstrip software spend. I think that people have not yet really internalized how much the physics around cybersecurity are going to change. I think there's to end up with a much more secure world.
Speaker 2 | 00:39 - 01:02 Hi, listeners. Welcome back to No Priors. Today, Elad and I talk with Greg Brockman, the cofounder and president of OpenAI. We discuss OpenAI's latest math results, Astra, and why Greg believes AI can now generate genuinely new knowledge. We get into drug discovery dots and his case for why security spending should actually vastly outstrip software spending, which is quite a claim.
Speaker 2 | 01:02 - 01:06 Here's our conversation with Greg Brockmiff. Greg, thanks so much for doing this.
Speaker 1 | 01:06 - 01:08 Thanks, Regina. Thank you for having me.
Speaker 3 | 01:08 - 01:25 So every week in AI feels like a year. And a lot's happened this week for OpenAI. You rolled out GPT-six to over a billion people, which is pretty amazing. There's some really exciting news that you have on the math side. There's all sorts of things that undoubtedly that are happening internally.
Speaker 3 | 01:25 - 01:29 What are you most excited about that's happening right now, both at OpenAI and in the broader AI world? Look, I
Speaker 1 | 01:29 - 02:36 think that in AI, like I have this belief about how OpenAI operates, that there's this cycling quote of it never gets easier, you just go faster, and I think that's very much what happens is that there's just so much activity and that every time you think you're at peak impact and how things are happening, realize that there's actually another level that's possible and it's not just about any one company, it's not just about any one technology, it's really we as a world and society are all coming together to adopt this technology, get the most out of it, to improve everyone's lives. And so I think to me, the math results this week represent a real milestone, right? It's a real moment where if you think about the fundamental driver of human quality of life improving over the past thousand years is technology, right? It's scientific advancement and I think that we now have the ability to massively accelerate scientific discovery and there has always been this question of is AI actually able to come up with new knowledge and at this point, it's just impossible to deny, right? It is definitively, yes, possible.
Speaker 1 | 02:36 - 03:17 Now there is still more to go. I think we not yet coming up with whole, brand new theories, but we are able to resolve these 100 year old math problems and to me, the thing that is very exciting is it is not just about the machine just sort of gives you an answer, right? It's really what can a human equipped with these tools achieve that was unthinkable before and I think it's almost like the leverage of humans to do whatever you want to do, it's going way, way up, right? It's now that you can, if you have a math problem you want go solve, you can solve it, but what about taking that same capability and applying it to biology? What about if you're a small business owner and you want to be able to operate your business well?
Speaker 1 | 03:17 - 03:32 Like that level of intelligence that's tuned for that domain, it's just going to mean that almost this sort of unthinkable results that are aligned with your goals, with your desires, is now going to be within the breach of everyone and that to me is so exciting.
Speaker 3 | 03:32 - 04:07 The RADAR progress has been pretty amazing too because if I look at it, you you used to have problems with arithmetic, right, in early models, I remember people complain, oh, why can't it do basic math? And now you're solving these advanced theorems. As these things continue to advance and starts to really impact areas of math, physics, materials, etcetera, and various applications, there some need if these models get so smart to focus on how to communicate that effectively to people? Or how do you think about the actual communication side of this as you do a very advanced theorem? Because if you look at any field of math, only a very small number of people can ever really adjudicate a theorem that's produced by a person.
Speaker 3 | 04:07 - 04:10 Yes. Right? And so you kind of have this specialization that happens.
Speaker 1 | 04:10 - 05:13 Well, and this, by the way, is something that has always been, like I came from a math background, like I thought I was going to be a mathematician and I was very inspired by mathematicians like Galois or Gauss, right, these people who were working on like a one hundred, four hundred year time horizon, right, and I think there's something deeply beautiful about mathematics being about sort of understanding the structure of the universe and so it's not just about and there's always these questions about is math invented or discovered and that in my mind it's something that the beauty and the meaning of mathematics, it's not something that is objective in some sense, in the eye of the beholder, it's something that appeals to us and there is some amount that's like physical laws and it's about simplicity and, you know, complexity theory and all these things that are maybe more physics but there is something that is also importantly human about it and so to me, it's not just about, I think a lot of the conversation about mathematics, it's not just about here's a proof, no one understands it, great, we resolve the problem.
Speaker 1 | 05:13 - 06:21 It's really about what are the insights that are derived and the thing that I think we will see, but I think that there's promising signs of life on, is that there are beautiful insights within the work that these AIs have done and I think what we're seeing right now is that, you know, we published about almost 400 very important open problems that are now resolved and the mathematical community is going through all of that to look for insights and if you read some of the things that people have posted, domain experts in these particular problems and they say that it's like there is these almost like sort of very surprising ways of applying ideas or incredibly like, wait, why did they use that result over here and that what's coming out is not these incomprehensible theorem or the proofs which, by the way, there is a history of incomprehensible proofs in mathematics. Like, four color theorem is a perfect example of this that is, it's like, okay, we just had the machine check a bunch of cases, like there's no beauty in that. And so I think we're into a different phase of machine discovery.
Speaker 2 | 06:21 - 06:43 I have some optimism that, like, as models also get to better theory of mind, like the ability to figure out, like, what we as humans know and how to get us to follow them on the path to new understanding will also be paved. Right? And and so, like, for example, like, I'm a a math person, but at some point in school, I stopped learning math. And then I did math academy. And then I did, like, chat GPT to help me learn new math.
Speaker 2 | 06:43 - 06:52 And so I just feel like the expectation for, you know, the rising tide of what knowledge, like, you can expect people to understand will also be there.
Speaker 1 | 06:52 - 07:46 I think that this is a really important point and one of maybe the underappreciated benefits that I expect from and hope for and are starting to see from this technology is helping...
